title: Glanzmann vs Bernard-Soulier: Reading Platelet Aggregation
summary: Meet the two platelet receptors that build a plug, watch light transmission aggregometry clear the plasma, and learn the mirror-image patterns of Glanzmann thrombasthenia and Bernard-Soulier syndrome.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 37 Hit 1 (core: Glanzmann vs Bernard-Soulier), Hit 4 and Trap 5 (agglutination vs aggregation terminology) and the Figure 37 memory anchor. Checked against Palma-Barqueros 2021 and Le Blanc 2020. Pending: the reviewer’s statement that ristocetin agglutination works with fixed platelets.

objectives: Describe the roles of GPIb-IX-V and GPIIb-IIIa in adhesion and aggregation.
Interpret light transmission aggregometry patterns in Glanzmann thrombasthenia and Bernard-Soulier syndrome.
Distinguish Bernard-Soulier syndrome from severe von Willebrand disease with a plasma correction.

scenes.title: Two bleeders, two missing receptors
scenes.altText: Two patients with lifelong mucosal bleeding. Patient 1 has a normal platelet count with normal-sized platelets. Patient 2 has a low count with giant platelets. A platelet cartoon shows two receptors on its surface: GPIIb-IIIa (αIIbβ3) and GPIb-IX-V. One patient lacks each.

cues.text: Two patients have bled easily all their lives — nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy bruising.
One has a normal platelet count with normal-looking platelets. The other has a low count with giant platelets.
Each is missing a different platelet receptor. Platelet aggregation testing tells you which.

scenes.title: Normal: two receptors, two jobs
scenes.altText: A platelet at a damaged vessel wall. First, GPIb-IX-V grabs von Willebrand factor (vWF) stuck to the wall — adhesion. Then, once activated, GPIIb-IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3) binds fibrinogen bridges between platelets — aggregation into a plug. A light-transmission aggregometer is then shown: platelet-rich plasma in a cuvette turns clearer as platelets clump and light passes through.

cues.text: Platelets need two key receptors. GPIb-IX-V is the receptor for von Willebrand factor. It lets platelets stick to an injured vessel wall.
GPIIb-IIIa, also called integrin alpha-two-b beta-three, links activated platelets to each other through fibrinogen bridges. That builds the plug.
The lab tests this with light transmission aggregometry, the reference test for platelet function. An agonist is added to platelet-rich plasma.
As platelets clump, the cloudy plasma clears and more light passes through. The rise in light transmission is the aggregation response.

scenes.title: What changes: mirror-image patterns
scenes.altText: Three result columns. Normal: ✓ ADP, collagen, arachidonic acid, ristocetin. Glanzmann thrombasthenia (no GPIIb-IIIa): ✗ ADP, ✗ collagen, ✗ arachidonic acid, ✓ ristocetin (normal or reduced second wave); normal count and morphology; clot retraction absent. Bernard-Soulier syndrome (no GPIb-IX-V): ✓ ADP, collagen, arachidonic acid (normal or reduced), ✗ ristocetin; thrombocytopenia with giant platelets. Both are autosomal recessive.

cues.text: A normal sample responds to every agonist.

In Glanzmann thrombasthenia, GPIIb-IIIa is missing. Platelets can’t bridge to each other, so aggregation to ADP, collagen and arachidonic acid is absent — but the response to ristocetin is normal. Count and size are normal, and clot retraction is absent.
Bernard-Soulier syndrome is the mirror image. GPIb-IX-V is missing, so ristocetin gives no response, while the other agonists work. And the platelets are few and giant.
Both are inherited autosomal recessively, and flow cytometry can show the missing receptor directly.

props.label: Both autosomal recessive · flow cytometry shows the missing receptor

scenes.title: In the lab: is it the receptor or the factor?
scenes.altText: Absent ristocetin response has two main explanations: no GPIb-IX-V on the platelets (Bernard-Soulier) or no von Willebrand factor in the plasma (severe von Willebrand disease). A correction experiment adds normal plasma (which contains vWF): in severe VWD the ristocetin response returns; in Bernard-Soulier it does not. Ristocetin’s response is called agglutination; the other agonists cause aggregation.

cues.text: A missing ristocetin response doesn’t automatically mean Bernard-Soulier. Severe von Willebrand disease also abolishes it — the receptor is fine, but its partner, von Willebrand factor, is missing.
So add normal plasma, which supplies von Willebrand factor. In severe von Willebrand disease, the ristocetin response comes back.
In Bernard-Soulier syndrome it doesn’t — no amount of factor helps if the receptor is absent.
One more word to get right: ristocetin causes agglutination, through von Willebrand factor and GPIb. The other agonists cause aggregation.

scenes.title: Two classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Giant platelets + low count = ITP, transfuse” is crossed out → “Think Bernard-Soulier: check the ristocetin response and receptor expression.” Trap card: “Absent ristocetin response = Bernard-Soulier” is crossed out → “Severe VWD does it too; normal plasma corrects VWD, not BSS.”

cues.text: Trap one: a low count with giant platelets isn’t automatically immune thrombocytopenia. Bernard-Soulier syndrome looks like that too. Check the ristocetin response and the receptor by flow cytometry.
Trap two: an absent ristocetin response isn’t automatically Bernard-Soulier. Severe von Willebrand disease does the same. Normal plasma corrects von Willebrand disease, not Bernard-Soulier.
And in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, the count, size and ristocetin response are all normal — only aggregation is missing.

scenes.title: Glanzmann can’t glue; Bernard can’t grab
scenes.altText: Memory aid: Glanzmann can’t GLUE platelets together (no GPIIb-IIIa → no aggregation, ristocetin fine). Bernard-Soulier can’t GRAB the wall (no GPIb → no ristocetin, and Big platelets). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: Glanzmann can’t glue — no GPIIb-IIIa, so platelets won’t stick to each other, but ristocetin still works. Bernard can’t grab — no GPIb, so platelets can’t grab von Willebrand factor, ristocetin fails, and the platelets are big.

Where it breaks: partial and variant forms give weaker patterns, reagent concentrations differ between labs, severe von Willebrand disease mimics Bernard-Soulier on ristocetin, and medications can blunt aggregation. Flow cytometry and genetics confirm.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Glanzmann: no GPIIb-IIIa → no aggregation; ristocetin normal”, “Bernard-Soulier: no GPIb → no ristocetin; giant platelets, low count”, “Normal plasma corrects severe VWD, not BSS”.

cues.text: Glanzmann thrombasthenia lacks GPIIb-IIIa, so platelets fail to aggregate but respond to ristocetin, while Bernard-Soulier syndrome lacks GPIb and shows the mirror image with giant platelets.

props.label: Glanzmann: no GPIIb-IIIa → no aggregation · ristocetin normal
Bernard-Soulier: no GPIb → no ristocetin · giant platelets
Normal plasma corrects severe VWD, not BSS

explanation.what: Plain language: platelets need one receptor to stick to an injured wall and another to stick to each other; each rare inherited disorder removes one. Scientific terms: Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GT) lacks or has defective αIIbβ3 (GPIIb-IIIa); Bernard-Soulier syndrome (BSS) lacks the GPIb-IX-V complex, the main vWF receptor.
explanation.why: Without αIIbβ3, platelets cannot form fibrinogen bridges, so aggregation to ADP, collagen, arachidonic acid and thrombin is absent or severely reduced, while ristocetin agglutination (vWF–GPIb) is normal or has a reduced second wave; clot retraction is absent. Without GPIb-IX-V, ristocetin agglutination is absent and not corrected by normal plasma, other agonists are normal or reduced, and there is thrombocytopenia with giant platelets.
explanation.measure: Light transmission aggregometry (LTA), the reference platelet-function test: an agonist is added to platelet-rich plasma and aggregation is measured as increased light transmission. Flow cytometry shows the missing receptor; adding normal plasma distinguishes severe VWD (corrects) from BSS (does not).
explanation.differs: GT (normal count and size, no aggregation, ristocetin preserved) vs BSS (low count, giant platelets, no ristocetin response); BSS vs severe VWD (normal plasma corrects VWD only); agglutination (ristocetin) vs aggregation (other agonists).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: an aggregation table to match to GT or BSS, the giant-platelet trap, the plasma correction for BSS vs VWD, and agglutination vs aggregation wording.

mnemonic.text: Glanzmann can’t glue; Bernard can’t grab.
mnemonic.explanation: Glanzmann lacks the “glue” receptor (GPIIb-IIIa) for platelet–platelet aggregation; Bernard-Soulier lacks the “grab” receptor (GPIb) for vWF, so ristocetin fails and platelets are big.
mnemonic.limitation: Variant forms give milder patterns, agonist concentrations differ between labs, severe VWD mimics BSS on ristocetin, and drugs can blunt aggregation; flow cytometry and genetics confirm.

takeaway: Glanzmann thrombasthenia lacks GPIIb-IIIa, so platelets fail to aggregate but respond to ristocetin, while Bernard-Soulier syndrome lacks GPIb and shows the mirror image with giant platelets.

questions.stem: A child with lifelong mucosal bleeding has a normal platelet count and size. Aggregation is absent with ADP, collagen and arachidonic acid, but normal with ristocetin. Which disorder fits best?

options.rationale: Correct. Missing αIIbβ3 abolishes aggregation to these agonists while ristocetin agglutination is preserved.
Incorrect. BSS shows absent ristocetin response with low count and giant platelets.
Incorrect. Severe VWD abolishes the ristocetin response.
Incorrect. The platelet count is normal.

questions.stem: A patient with thrombocytopenia and giant platelets has no ristocetin response. Adding normal plasma does not restore it. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Correct. The GPIb-IX-V receptor is absent, so supplying vWF does not help.
Incorrect. Normal plasma supplies vWF and would restore the response in VWD.
Incorrect. GT has a normal ristocetin response and normal-sized platelets.
Incorrect. An absent ristocetin response is abnormal.

questions.stem: Which receptor is defective in Glanzmann thrombasthenia?

options.rationale: Correct. It binds fibrinogen to link platelets during aggregation.
Incorrect. That is the vWF receptor missing in Bernard-Soulier syndrome.
Incorrect. P2Y12 is an ADP receptor; its defect affects ADP responses selectively.
Incorrect. GPVI is a collagen receptor.

claims.text: GT: normal count/size, absent aggregation to ADP, collagen, AA/TxA2, thrombin; ristocetin normal (or reduced second wave); absent clot retraction; AR.
BSS: thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, absent ristocetin agglutination not corrected by normal plasma (unlike severe VWD); other agonists normal or reduced; AR.
LTA is the reference test; aggregation measured as increased light transmission in PRP after an agonist; agonist doses vary by guideline.
Ristocetin response is termed agglutination; other agonists cause aggregation.
Ristocetin agglutination is passive and works on fixed (metabolically inactive) platelets.
claims.note: Not taught; not stated in the sources read.

claims.text: GPIb-IX-V mediates adhesion to vWF at the injured wall; αIIbβ3 links activated platelets via fibrinogen.
claims.note: Standard physiology consistent with the sources (vWF receptor; αIIbβ3/fibrinogen binding) but not stated as such in the passages read.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer says ristocetin response is preserved in GT; Palma-Barqueros 2021 notes it is normal or has a reduced second wave. The lesson says “normal (or reduced second wave)”.
